questions.q: At its root, is a move a step across the 15 squares (5 channels by 3 satisfaction states), or an action a character takes?
questions.why_you: You listed channels, states, sheng, ke, faces and daemons, but said the nature of a move is still being figured out. The record has both readings: move-engine treats a move as a pair of elements, and your spirit-fight rulings treat moves like Pokemon moves people teach.
questions.not_before: Nobody had laid the nine meanings of 'move' side by side until this audit (council/research/2026-10-19-move-audit.md).

options.label: A. A step across the 15 squares (recommended)
options.c: One table of fifteen moves becomes the engine for every game; faces and daemons decide which step to offer and how it sounds. All five faces back this.

options.label: B. A character's action
options.c: Each face, daemon and spirit carries its own moves, and moving across the squares is one effect among others (damage, comfort, reveal). More variety, harder to keep games in step.

options.label: C. Both, kept as two layers
options.c: The squares are the engine and actions are named skins on top; a Pokemon-style move always maps to one step. Most work up front.

questions.q: What does a control (ke) move do to how satisfied a channel is?
questions.why_you: Five surfaces disagree: move-engine and the check-in lower it one step, the Sprout slice and alchemy-graph hold it, the ontology game keeps a satisfied channel satisfied, and your ruling ea13b says ke acts only by releasing grip. Only you can say which feels true to the practice.
questions.not_before: Each surface was built separately; this is the first time they were compared.

options.label: A. Holds it; ke releases grip (recommended)
options.c: Matches your ea13b ruling and the slice. Control never punishes; it loosens what is stuck. move-engine's -1 changes.

options.label: B. Lowers it one step
options.c: Matches move-engine. Control has a cost, which gives fights tension, and Temper Action reads as a sacrifice.

options.label: C. Depends on where you start
options.c: Like the Sprout prototype: from satisfied it holds, from neutral it pulls back. Richer, and needs a table per state.

questions.q: How do the game master faces and the daemons attach to moves?
questions.why_you: faces.yaml ties no face to a move, while bars-engine has four face-to-move maps that disagree, and daemons' home elements in Sprout appear nowhere in the council record. This is a design preference only you hold.
questions.not_before: The four maps grew in separate features; nobody compared them before this audit.

options.label: A. Faces voice any move; daemons have habits (recommended)
options.c: Any face can offer any move in its own register. Each daemon has a home channel and a move it reaches for when dissatisfied, and teaches moves once it is an ally. bars-engine's four maps collapse to one.

options.label: B. Each face and daemon owns its moves
options.c: Like lens-moves: each face has three moves. Clear identities, and some moves (Temper Action today) belong to no one.

options.label: C. Settle the kernel first
options.c: Rule A or B after the move table exists and you have played it.
